      {"@context":"http://schema.org","@graph":[{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-07-16T22:51:14.756Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_one-site-providing-state-homes-since-1972-activity-7483654510058504192-yfup","text":"One site providing state homes since 1972 

In Ōtara, we’ve replaced 10 ageing homes that have housed families since the 1970s with 18 new, modern homes right next door to a primary school and close to shops, healthcare and essential services. 

With strong demand for larger family homes in the area, this development includes: 
• 6 five-bedroom homes 
• 6 three-bedroom homes 
• 6 two-bedroom homes. 

The redevelopment of the site is part of our nationwide work to replace older homes with new ones that better meet our tenants’ needs while also making better use of existing land. ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_one-site-providing-state-homes-since-1972-activity-7483654510058504192-yfup"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-07-09T03:44:52.974Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_stable-housing-helping-children-thrive-activity-7480829303321030656-iBIa","text":"Stable housing helping children thrive ✅

 Fifteen new homes have replaced five older state houses across two sites in Bryndwr, Christchurch. 

The 11 two-bedroom and 4 three-bedroom homes are close to schools, public transport and community facilities. 

Local Burnside Primary School Principal Justin Perriam says the new homes will make a real difference for families. 

 “Having access to stable, affordable housing gives families the opportunity to truly put down roots. When children can stay in the same school, they build lasting friendships, develop strong relationships with their teachers, and have the support required for academic success. 

 “Too often we've seen whānau forced to move because private rental properties are sold, disrupting children's learning and wellbeing. Developments like this provide much-needed stability, allowing families to belong, participate, and thrive within both our school and wider community.” ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_stable-housing-helping-children-thrive-activity-7480829303321030656-iBIa"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-07-02T21:18:15.225Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_a-significant-milestone-for-nelson-with-16-activity-7478557677711884288-zpKR","text":"A significant milestone for Nelson with 16 new state homes now complete and families set to move in from later this week. 

The new development includes 6 two-bedroom and 10 three-bedroom homes and was blessed earlier this week. Te Pouahi ākonga (students) from nearby Nelson Central School helped to mark the occasion with waiata. 

Nelson Central School Principal Pip Wells highlighted the wider impact of quality housing on education and wellbeing: 

“We know that a child’s learning doesn't start at the classroom door - it starts at home and our presence at the blessing underpins our support for this new social housing project in our neighbourhood.  

“When tamariki transition into warm, stable, purpose-built homes, the benefits to their education are profound. We see healthier kids, fewer sickness-related absences, and an end to the disruptive cycle of constantly changing schools.” 

The site also holds cultural significance for iwi. This is represented on the site through the incorporation of cultural design elements, including tāniko patterns and a tuna motif. We worked with Ngāti Tama worked during the design phase to bring these elements to life.  

The homes were delivered as part of our renewals programme, which will see around 2000 older homes replaced or extensively renovated nationwide each year over the next few years. ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_a-significant-milestone-for-nelson-with-16-activity-7478557677711884288-zpKR"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-06-30T23:20:08.481Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_projects-like-this-allow-us-to-give-back-activity-7477863576007958528-7Xr7","text":"“Projects like this allow us to give back to the community we live and work in.” 

For Jennian Homes Managing Director Frank O’Toole working on a new state housing development in Westport enables his company to reinvest in the West Coast town.  

Four one-bedroom and 6 two-bedroom homes across two sites were blessed by iwi Ngāti Waewae last week. Tenants are now beginning to move in. 

Frank says the project has helped to provide reliable work for his team and local subcontractors and suppliers. “We typically have 10-15 people on site each day.  It has really kept a lot of people in good solid work. 

“We live in a great part of the country, and we love being able to support our community through sports and other sponsorships.” 

Frank says his team is also proud to work on homes for people in need. “We’re really pleased to be involved in a project that helps to relieve some of the pressure by moving people off waiting lists and into homes.” 

The builds are part of our housing renewals programme, which is replacing or significantly upgrading around 2,000 older homes nationwide each year. 
 ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_projects-like-this-allow-us-to-give-back-activity-7477863576007958528-7Xr7"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-06-25T01:56:20.308Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_ruvi-community-development-and-engagement-activity-7475728557076365313-PgLK","text":"RUVI | Community Development and Engagement Manager 

“12 years ago, I was tired, cold and nursing a sprained ankle all alone at a Los Angeles bus stop. 

I knew that’s not what I was here for, so I made a conscious decision to change. 

I was born in Kandy, Sri Lanka, my mum and grandmother raised me while my dad worked in California, USA, sending money home. My grandmother, a respected teacher, always modelled care and inclusion in our home. 

It was the 90s and my childhood was perforated by the Sri Lankan civil war. I would be escorted to school by soldiers, bombs going off, and one time a nearby blast was so shocking that it knocked me from my bed. 

But it was such a strong community. We had Buddhist kids, Muslim kids, Tamil kids, Christian kids…we would all come together. It was a great place and I still have good friends there.

That sense of belonging disappeared at 11 years old when we moved to La Crescenta, California, to join my dad. 

After high school I moved on to university where I studied finance while working full time at a credit union, and later graduated with a Business Degree. A few challenging events happened in my early twenties and things became too much. Piece by piece everything came crashing down.  

By 23, I was homeless on the streets of LA. It was days without food… days without having a place to sleep. When it comes to being alone, that was as alone as you could kind of get. For years, I lived on the streets. There were people dying. People overdosing. Constant chaos. I would occasionally try to get back up on my feet, but the decisions I made and the environment that surrounded me never allowed for success. 

But I still had kind of a moral guidance… I wasn’t there to hurt anybody, I had just given up on myself. That moral grounding helped me step away before it was too late. 

After moving to join my sister in Aotearoa, New Zealand, I worked for Y Central (YMCA) in Wellington. The next eight years were filled with a variety of roles before working my way up to the Senior Leadership Team as the Area Manager. My favourite project was helping to establish Te Tai Ohinga, a great space just for rangatahi to come together in a safe environment. 

That guidance and my own lived experience deeply inform my work today. 
It’s about helping to give people a chance for a better life. The most important thing is just keep showing up for them. That’s probably something they’re not used to - people just being there for them. 

We had an area where we needed to work with some disengaged tenants to address disruptive behaviour. Through consistent support and partnerships, we saw this community begin to shift.  

By the end of that year, it had changed… they loved to see us there. The kids and families were happy. Those are the moments that matter. If you can help somebody, you help somebody. 

I love where I am right now. Everything that has happened in my life has brought me to this moment and I’m lucky to be here.”","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_ruvi-community-development-and-engagement-activity-7475728557076365313-PgLK"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-06-24T02:41:10.449Z","headline":"","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_right-size-homes-for-tenant-needs-our-activity-7475377452513464320-9qaa","text":"Right size homes for tenant needs 🙌 
 
Our Counties Manukau team is currently placing tenants into 14 newly completed family homes in Māngere, South Auckland. The homes are mostly four, five and six‑bedroom homes and are located near schools, parks, public transport, shops, and the hospital.
 
Our placements team is working with high‑priority applicants, including those on MSD’s housing register, tenants whose circumstances have changed, and they now need a bigger home, households moving from transitional housing into a permanent home, and people relocating through redevelopment.
 
Ahead of tenants moving in, the homes were blessed and local stakeholders were invited to visit the completed development. More than 60 people came along, and we received positive feedback about the design, layout of the homes and their great location.
 
This development is part of our renewals programme where we’re replacing older homes that are no longer suitable for social housing with new homes that are the right size for our tenants and better meet their needs. By the end of this month, we’ll have delivered almost 100 new homes in this area, and we’re planning to deliver an additional 82 new homes next year.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_right-size-homes-for-tenant-needs-our-activity-7475377452513464320-9qaa"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-06-21T23:00:24.404Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_as-ai-use-grows-there-is-increasing-risk-activity-7474597118838620160-k2tq","text":""As AI use grows, there is increasing risk that indigenous knowledge becomes decontextualised, undermining trust.” 
 
The recent 2026 Government Innovation Showcase highlighted that innovation in Aotearoa does not happen in isolation, but within the context of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. 

 

Our Deputy Chief Executive Group Māori, Te Ariki Pihama, made the case for grounding innovation in mātauranga Māori. 

Te Ariki leads Te Kurutao Group Māori, who help us support Māori housing aspirations by supporting tikanga across the organisation, strengthening Māori/Crown relationships, and growing staff cultural capability. 
 
Te Ariki’s insights on applying mātauranga Māori, kaitiakitanga and stewardship to data, emphasised real progress comes not from faster tools but from wiser use of them.  

“The key advice for many of us is to remain mindful of who it relates to and how they would like us to use it. We have to ensure our use of data looks beyond short-term outputs to long-term outcomes. When that data relates to people, communities and mātauranga Māori, it should be treated as taonga, with the responsibility of kaitiakitanga guiding how it is used.” ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_as-ai-use-grows-there-is-increasing-risk-activity-7474597118838620160-k2tq"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-06-12T03:26:55.395Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_we-delivered-203-homes-in-may-from-as-far-activity-7471040311218241536-Aipv","text":"We delivered 203 homes in May, from as far North as Whangarei and as far South as Dunedin. 

May marked a turning point for dozens of whānau across the country, as they moved into new homes that will bring them greater stability and a new sense of belonging. 

“I’m really looking forward to making a home here for me and my moko,’’ says a tenant who moved into one of eight new homes opened in Gisborne. After six years living in a caravan, she can finally ‘cook properly and sit at a table’. 

"It’s nice to be somewhere warm and have my own space again, it just feels good," says a tenant who moved into one of 16 new homes in New Plymouth.

Some of our other delivery highlights for May include: 

- Adding 8 two-bedroom homes in Greymouth which were built off site in partnership with Department of Corrections NZ, supporting skills development and rehabilitation. 
-35 homes were significantly renovated, adding at least 50 years to their lifespan as part of our retrofit programme.

June is going to be another busy month of deliveries as we continue to renew our housing stock.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_we-delivered-203-homes-in-may-from-as-far-activity-7471040311218241536-Aipv"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-06-11T02:47:00.062Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_dayne-community-development-and-engagement-activity-7470667876639780864-gOgl","text":"DAYNE | Community Development and Engagement Manager at Te Mātāwai 

“I’ve never met anyone where I think, why are you like that? There’s always a reason. I think we should all make an effort to understand where people come from. 
 
I remember what Ronnie, a streetie (a homeless person), told me years ago.  
 
“Humans are like trees. All you see is what's above ground, but you don't see the root system underneath and what's raised that tree up. That root system is twice as big as what you see above ground.” 
 
That stayed with me as it reinforced something I already felt. Once you understand someone’s backstory, it’s hard to judge them. 
 
I call Avondale home. It’s where my mum was born and raised, and now it’s where I’m raising my own family with my partner and our three kids. I’ve got a mixed background, my mum is of Samoan and Cook Islands descent, and my dad is of Irish and English descent. 
 
A lot of what I do today goes back to my upbringing. My mum had a tough upbringing, and because of that she raised us with a strong sense of perspective. She volunteered with the Māori Women’s Welfare League and later became a social worker. She’d often say, “You guys are lucky. Other people have it tough.” 
 
It wasn’t like she sat us down and intentionally taught us lessons, but that message was constant. I took it on board and realised I was relatively privileged compared to many people in my family and community. It shaped this feeling in me that I wanted to use what I had to benefit others. 
 
My pathway wasn’t straightforward. I went to university straight out of school at 17, first in my family to do so. I was studying computer science because that’s what my dad suggested, but it didn’t fit. After one semester I bombed out and spent a few years lost, moving from place to place, living on the benefit and tryna figure things out. By my mid-20s I’d explored enough side streets to know the right path was giving uni another go and I ended up with a degree in media studies and sociology from the University of Auckland.  
 
Before joining Kāinga Ora about five years ago, I founded I Love Avondale, a community development initiative that started as a social media platform that we collectively grew into a registered charity. We focused on storytelling, community food projects and opportunities for youth. That work led me into my current role helping shape Te Mātāwai.
 
My role is about building relationships and trust. I’m not there as an authority or expert telling people what to do, I see myself as a peer. I spend time with people, get to know them, understand their strengths and aspirations. 
 
The work can be challenging. There’s a lot of people navigating addiction and difficult pasts, but I grew up around similar environments, so I understand it and I’m not naive to it. I know this is what we signed up for.

What keeps me going is seeing change. It might start small, but over time it builds - a snowball effect."

Continued in the comments 👇 ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_dayne-community-development-and-engagement-activity-7470667876639780864-gOgl"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora"},"datePublished":"2026-06-10T04:51:08.265Z","headline":"","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_the-largest-social-housing-project-delivered-activity-7470336728810270720-HijY","text":"The largest social housing project delivered in regional New Zealand is now complete!

This 95-home development in Whangarei will provide housing for around 320 people!
 
Many of the new residents are moving from homelessness, emergency or transitional housing into these long-term, stable homes. The development has a mix of housing types, including accessible ground floor homes, and is located close to essential services to support better day to day living. 
 
Partnership has been central to this project - with local hapu Te Parawhau providing ongoing support and cultural leadership, including the naming of Kanae Way and the Whare Awhina community space, a place designed to bring residents together. 
 
The homes were architecturally designed and developed by Phoenix Properties and built by Loveridge Builders, with more than 120 tradespeople contributing over the 36-month build.  

The project brings the total of new state homes delivered in Whangārei in the past three years to 300. 
 
Northland is an area of high housing need with hundreds of people on MSD’s housing register. This development reflects our continued commitment to renewing our aging portfolio of social housing and delivering quality homes in areas of greatest need.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kainga-ora_the-largest-social-housing-project-delivered-activity-7470336728810270720-HijY"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"Organization","name":"Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/kainga-ora","address":{"type":"PostalAddress","streetAddress":"7 Waterloo Quay","addressLocality":"Wellington","addressRegion":"Wellington Region","postalCode":"6011","addressCountry":"NZ"},"description":"Kāinga Ora provides social housing and support to individuals and families across New Zealand.     <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">A significant milestone for Nelson with 16 new state homes now complete and families set to move in from later this week. 

The new development includes 6 two-bedroom and 10 three-bedroom homes and was blessed earlier this week. Te Pouahi ākonga (students) from nearby Nelson Central School helped to mark the occasion with waiata. 

Nelson Central School Principal Pip Wells highlighted the wider impact of quality housing on education and wellbeing: 

“We know that a child’s learning doesn't start at the classroom door - it starts at home and our presence at the blessing underpins our support for this new social housing project in our neighbourhood.  

“When tamariki transition into warm, stable, purpose-built homes, the benefits to their education are profound. We see healthier kids, fewer sickness-related absences, and an end to the disruptive cycle of constantly changing schools.” 

The site also holds cultural significance for iwi. This is represented on the site through the incorporation of cultural design elements, including tāniko patterns and a tuna motif. We worked with Ngāti Tama worked during the design phase to bring these elements to life.  

The homes were delivered as part of our renewals programme, which will see around 2000 older homes replaced or extensively renovated nationwide each year over the next few years. </p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">“Projects like this allow us to give back to the community we live and work in.”

Four one-bedroom and 6 two-bedroom homes across two sites were blessed by iwi Ngāti Waewae last week. Tenants are now beginning to move in. 

Frank says the project has helped to provide reliable work for his team and local subcontractors and suppliers. “We typically have 10-15 people on site each day.  It has really kept a lot of people in good solid work. 

“We live in a great part of the country, and we love being able to support our community through sports and other sponsorships.” 

Frank says his team is also proud to work on homes for people in need. “We’re really pleased to be involved in a project that helps to relieve some of the pressure by moving people off waiting lists and into homes.”

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">RUVI | Community Development and Engagement Manager 

“12 years ago, I was tired, cold and nursing a sprained ankle all alone at a Los Angeles bus stop. 

I knew that’s not what I was here for, so I made a conscious decision to change. 

I was born in Kandy, Sri Lanka, my mum and grandmother raised me while my dad worked in California, USA, sending money home. My grandmother, a respected teacher, always modelled care and inclusion in our home. 

It was the 90s and my childhood was perforated by the Sri Lankan civil war. I would be escorted to school by soldiers, bombs going off, and one time a nearby blast was so shocking that it knocked me from my bed. 

But it was such a strong community. We had Buddhist kids, Muslim kids, Tamil kids, Christian kids…we would all come together. It was a great place and I still have good friends there.

That sense of belonging disappeared at 11 years old when we moved to La Crescenta, California, to join my dad. 

After high school I moved on to university where I studied finance while working full time at a credit union, and later graduated with a Business Degree. A few challenging events happened in my early twenties and things became too much. Piece by piece everything came crashing down.  

By 23, I was homeless on the streets of LA. It was days without food… days without having a place to sleep. When it comes to being alone, that was as alone as you could kind of get. For years, I lived on the streets. There were people dying. People overdosing. Constant chaos. I would occasionally try to get back up on my feet, but the decisions I made and the environment that surrounded me never allowed for success. 

But I still had kind of a moral guidance… I wasn’t there to hurt anybody, I had just given up on myself. That moral grounding helped me step away before it was too late. 

After moving to join my sister in Aotearoa, New Zealand, I worked for <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/y-central-inc?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Y Central</a> (YMCA) in Wellington. The next eight years were filled with a variety of roles before working my way up to the Senior Leadership Team as the Area Manager. My favourite project was helping to establish Te Tai Ohinga, a great space just for rangatahi to come together in a safe environment. 

That guidance and my own lived experience deeply inform my work today. 
It’s about helping to give people a chance for a better life. The most important thing is just keep showing up for them. That’s probably something they’re not used to - people just being there for them. 

We had an area where we needed to work with some disengaged tenants to address disruptive behaviour. Through consistent support and partnerships, we saw this community begin to shift.  

By the end of that year, it had changed… they loved to see us there. The kids and families were happy. Those are the moments that matter. If you can help somebody, you help somebody. 

I love where I am right now. Everything that has happened in my life has brought me to this moment and I’m lucky to be here.”</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">"As AI use grows, there is increasing risk that indigenous knowledge becomes decontextualised, undermining trust.” 
 
The recent 2026 Government Innovation Showcase highlighted that innovation in Aotearoa does not happen in isolation, but within the context of Te Tiriti o Waitangi. 

 

Our Deputy Chief Executive Group Māori, Te Ariki Pihama, made the case for grounding innovation in mātauranga Māori. 

Te Ariki leads Te Kurutao Group Māori, who help us support Māori housing aspirations by supporting tikanga across the organisation, strengthening Māori/Crown relationships, and growing staff cultural capability. 
 
Te Ariki’s insights on applying mātauranga Māori, kaitiakitanga and stewardship to data, emphasised real progress comes not from faster tools but from wiser use of them.  

“The key advice for many of us is to remain mindful of who it relates to and how they would like us to use it. We have to ensure our use of data looks beyond short-term outputs to long-term outcomes. When that data relates to people, communities and mātauranga Māori, it should be treated as taonga, with the responsibility of kaitiakitanga guiding how it is used.” </p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We delivered 203 homes in May, from as far North as Whangarei and as far South as Dunedin. 

May marked a turning point for dozens of whānau across the country, as they moved into new homes that will bring them greater stability and a new sense of belonging. 

“I’m really looking forward to making a home here for me and my moko,’’ says a tenant who moved into one of eight new homes opened in Gisborne. After six years living in a caravan, she can finally ‘cook properly and sit at a table’. 

"It’s nice to be somewhere warm and have my own space again, it just feels good," says a tenant who moved into one of 16 new homes in New Plymouth.

Some of our other delivery highlights for May include: 

- Adding 8 two-bedroom homes in Greymouth which were built off site in partnership with Department of Corrections NZ, supporting skills development and rehabilitation. 
-35 homes were significantly renovated, adding at least 50 years to their lifespan as part of our retrofit programme.

June is going to be another busy month of deliveries as we continue to renew our housing stock.</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">DAYNE | Community Development and Engagement Manager at Te Mātāwai 

“I’ve never met anyone where I think, why are you like that? There’s always a reason. I think we should all make an effort to understand where people come from. 
 
I remember what Ronnie, a streetie (a homeless person), told me years ago.  
 
“Humans are like trees. All you see is what's above ground, but you don't see the root system underneath and what's raised that tree up. That root system is twice as big as what you see above ground.” 
 
That stayed with me as it reinforced something I already felt. Once you understand someone’s backstory, it’s hard to judge them. 
 
I call Avondale home. It’s where my mum was born and raised, and now it’s where I’m raising my own family with my partner and our three kids. I’ve got a mixed background, my mum is of Samoan and Cook Islands descent, and my dad is of Irish and English descent. 
 
A lot of what I do today goes back to my upbringing. My mum had a tough upbringing, and because of that she raised us with a strong sense of perspective. She volunteered with the Māori Women’s Welfare League and later became a social worker. She’d often say, “You guys are lucky. Other people have it tough.” 
 
It wasn’t like she sat us down and intentionally taught us lessons, but that message was constant. I took it on board and realised I was relatively privileged compared to many people in my family and community. It shaped this feeling in me that I wanted to use what I had to benefit others. 
 
My pathway wasn’t straightforward. I went to university straight out of school at 17, first in my family to do so. I was studying computer science because that’s what my dad suggested, but it didn’t fit. After one semester I bombed out and spent a few years lost, moving from place to place, living on the benefit and tryna figure things out. By my mid-20s I’d explored enough side streets to know the right path was giving uni another go and I ended up with a degree in media studies and sociology from the University of Auckland.  
 
Before joining Kāinga Ora about five years ago, I founded I Love Avondale, a community development initiative that started as a social media platform that we collectively grew into a registered charity. We focused on storytelling, community food projects and opportunities for youth. That work led me into my current role helping shape Te Mātāwai.
 
My role is about building relationships and trust. I’m not there as an authority or expert telling people what to do, I see myself as a peer. I spend time with people, get to know them, understand their strengths and aspirations. 
 
The work can be challenging. There’s a lot of people navigating addiction and difficult pasts, but I grew up around similar environments, so I understand it and I’m not naive to it. I know this is what we signed up for.

What keeps me going is seeing change. It might start small, but over time it builds - a snowball effect."

Continued in the comments 👇 </p>

        attributed-text-segment-list__content-truncated" dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">The largest social housing project delivered in regional New Zealand is now complete!

This 95-home development in Whangarei will provide housing for around 320 people!
 
Many of the new residents are moving from homelessness, emergency or transitional housing into these long-term, stable homes. The development has a mix of housing types, including accessible ground floor homes, and is located close to essential services to support better day to day living. 
 
Partnership has been central to this project - with local hapu Te Parawhau providing ongoing support and cultural leadership, including the naming of Kanae Way and the Whare Awhina community space, a place designed to bring residents together. 
 
The homes were architecturally designed and developed by Phoenix Properties and built by Loveridge Builders, with more than 120 tradespeople contributing over the 36-month build.  

The project brings the total of new state homes delivered in Whangārei in the past three years to 300. 
 
Northland is an area of high housing need with hundreds of people on MSD’s housing register. This development reflects our continued commitment to renewing our aging portfolio of social housing and delivering quality homes in areas of greatest need.</p>
